headline: A distinguished name can be read back from its string form, and twelve attributes the name table published can finally be encoded.
summary: Every parsed name carries `dn`, its string form, and nothing read one back, so a caller holding a distinguished name as text had to assemble the RDN structure by hand to sign anything with it. `pki.x509.parseDn` is the inverse. Building it surfaced two gaps behind it: twelve of the twenty-five attributes in the published short-name table resolved to no OID, so a name written with any of them could not be encoded at all, and a value the parser hands back in the `#`-prefixed or backslash-escaped form could not be fed back to the builder it came from.

Added: `pki.x509.parseDn(dn)` reads a distinguished-name string into `{ rdns, dn, bytes }`, using the attribute names and value escaping of RFC 4514 sections 2.4 and 3, including the `#`-prefixed hex form for a value whose ASN.1 type has no string form. `bytes` is raw `Name` DER, the form `spec.subject` and `spec.issuer` already take, so a name read from text can be signed without rebuilding it. Components are read in the order they are written, which is the order every `dn` here is emitted in and the order `openssl x509 -subject` prints; RFC 4514 section 2.1 specifies the opposite order, so a string from a directory tool that follows it names the components from last to first. Malformed input throws `x509/bad-dn`.

Twelve distinguished-name attributes are registered: `initials`, `generationQualifier`, `distinguishedNameQualifier`, `pseudonym`, `userId`, `businessCategory`, `postalCode`, `name`, `organizationIdentifier`, and the three CA/Browser Forum jurisdiction attributes. Each already had a short name in `pki.C.NAMES.DN_SHORT`, and `pki.oid.byName` returned undefined for all twelve, so `pki.x509.sign` refused a subject naming any of them.
Changed: The `dn` string of a name carrying one of those twelve attributes now labels it by name rather than by dotted OID, so a subject that read `2.5.4.15=Private Organization` reads `businessCategory=Private Organization`. The encoded certificate is unaffected; this is the rendered string, which `pki.inspect` and the `lint` findings also show.
Fixed: A string value beginning with U+FEFF keeps it. Reading a `UTF8String` went through a decoder that treats a leading U+FEFF as a byte-order mark and removes it, so the decoded value differed from the bytes that encoded it and two certificates whose subjects differed only by that character produced names that compared equal. X.690 gives U+FEFF no special meaning inside a string, and the same correction applies to the deterministic CBOR reader and the shared text decoder behind the protocol clients.

A `#`-prefixed attribute value is held to everything the plain string form is held to. It carries the value's own DER, so it previously bypassed the attribute's string type, its alphabet, its size bounds and the non-empty rule; a `countryName` of five characters, a `serialNumber` containing an underscore and an empty `commonName` could each be encoded that way and produced a name whose own emitted string would not parse. The supplied DER must now be the string type the attribute's module entry names, and its content is held to the same checks.

Four distinguished-name attributes are encoded with the ASN.1 string type their profile gives them, rather than as `UTF8String`: `domainComponent` and `emailAddress` as `IA5String`, and `distinguishedNameQualifier`, `serialNumber`, `countryName` and `jurisdictionCountryName` as `PrintableString`, the last two bounded to the two characters of a country code. A certificate carrying a `DC=` or `SERIALNUMBER=` component was non-conforming, and the alphabet each type restricts a value to was not applied, so a value those types cannot hold was accepted and encoded anyway. The size bounds the same module states are enforced with them: a `serialNumber` of 1 to 64 characters, an `emailAddress` of 1 to 255. Certificates already issued are unaffected; this changes the bytes newly issued ones carry.

`pki.x509.sign` accepts an attribute value in the two forms a parsed name hands back. A value whose type has no string form comes back as `#` followed by the hex of its DER, and a literal value beginning with `#` or a backslash comes back with a leading backslash; both were encoded as those literal characters instead of being read, so a name taken out of one certificate could not be written into another unchanged.
Documentation: Every obsoleted standards citation in README.md, ROADMAP.md and SECURITY.md names its successor beside it, so a reader is not sent to a number that is no longer current for its subject. Among them: RFC 4210 and RFC 9480 for CMP, now RFC 9810 and RFC 9811; RFC 5272, RFC 5273, RFC 5274 and RFC 6402 for CMC, now RFC 10002, RFC 10003 and RFC 10004; RFC 5019 for the lightweight OCSP profile, now RFC 9919; RFC 9579 for PBMAC1, now RFC 9879; RFC 8398 and RFC 8399 for internationalized names, now RFC 9598 and RFC 9549; RFC 2875 for Diffie-Hellman proof of possession, now RFC 6955; and RFC 8446 for TLS 1.3, now RFC 9846.

The roadmap's vulnerability table gains the CVE-2020-0601 row for the class refused at key import since 0.8.0, and states where the named-curve identifiers come from: RFC 5480 section 2.1.1.1 and RFC 5639 section 4.1, rather than the TLS cipher-suite document previously cited.
